description: For the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge, we aim to develop a data-driven solution that can analyze Earth system data, identify meaningful trends and patterns, and communicate findings through clear and effective visualizations.
summary:
EARTH//ORBIT (The Earth Detective Agency) is a 2D role-playing game built on more than 40 years of NASA satellite and reanalysis observations. Players investigate a mystery across all five layers of Earth’s atmosphere, from 0 km to 10,000 km. The central question is how a single physical process can produce opposite trends in different atmospheric regions. The game is aimed at high school students, university learners, educators, and citizen scientists, and it gives them a way into climate datasets that are otherwise large and disconnected.

Three scientific mentors guide the investigation: Dr. Nova, Commander Atlas, and ORBIT AI. Players work at interactive satellite consoles and run non-parametric Mann-Kendall significance tests and Theil-Sen slope estimators live in the browser. They then connect evidence from different layers on an interactive Evidence Wall to certify their final Earth System Dossier.
details:
1. The challenge: “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”

One physical process can push a measured variable up in one region and down in another. Earth’s vertical atmosphere shows this clearly.

In the troposphere (0-12 km), rising greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared radiation. This warms the lower atmosphere by 1.18 deg C and raises its water vapor capacity by about 7% per deg C. Higher up, in the stratosphere (12-50 km), mesosphere (50-85 km), and thermosphere (85-600 km), CO2 and nitric oxide (NO) radiate heat into space. The middle and upper atmosphere cool and contract, which pulls the exosphere (600-10,000 km) boundary downward.

Raw satellite tables and isolated papers do not show students and the public how these trends are linked physically and statistically. EARTH//ORBIT puts the player in the role of Steve, a Junior Detective at the Earth Detective Agency, who climbs through all five layers to investigate.

2. How it works: five layers, ten instruments, live statistics

Players walk a pixel-art orbital complex with WASD or arrow keys, mouse click-to-walk, or an on-screen mobile D-pad. They ride the Atmospheric Elevator to five stations.

At the EDA Ground Base (0 km), the Home Satellite Terminal and Main Bridge are where players detect the encrypted multi-layer anomaly signal and get clearance from Commander Atlas.

At the Troposphere Sky-Station (0-12 km), the Weather Signal Scanner (1A) and AIRS Profile Lab (1B) cover warming and moisture trends in the Tropical Pacific, Arctic Basin, and Bay of Bengal, plus lapse rates (-6.0 deg C/km). Completing them unlocks Card 01.

At the Stratosphere Ozone Lab (12-50 km), the Ozone Console (2A) and Mann-Kendall Trend Lab (2B) let players slice 1979-2025 ozone and temperature series, comparing CFC depletion with Montreal Protocol recovery, and run live Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen tests. This unlocks Card 02.

At the Mesosphere Observatory (50-85 km), the SABER Receiver (3A) and Missing Data Console (3B) show mesopause cooling (-1.8 deg C/decade) and document the 32% satellite limb-sampling gap. This unlocks Card 03.

At the Thermosphere Orbital Deck (85-600 km), the TIMED/GOLD Tracker (4A) and Aurora Comparator (4B) separate 11-year solar EUV and auroral cycles from long-term neutral density contraction (-3.8%/decade) across the overlapping ionosphere. This unlocks Card 04.

At the Exosphere Complex (600-10,000 km), the Geocorona Scanner (5A), Exobase Analyzer (5B), and Vault cover the ultraviolet hydrogen geocorona and exobase contraction (-12.5 km/decade), which unlocks Card 05. Players then link all five layers on the Evidence Wall and submit the Final Report.

3. The statistical engine

Instrument 2B runs non-parametric trend tests live in JavaScript as players switch between time windows (1979-1997, 2000-2025, or 1979-2025). The Mann-Kendall statistic (S) compares every earlier observation with every later one to find the trend direction. The standardized statistic (Z) and two-tailed p-value then show whether the trend is significant (p < 0.001) or within natural variability. The Theil-Sen estimator takes the median of all pairwise slopes to give a rate of change per decade, which keeps short-term outliers such as the 1982 El Chichon and 1991 Mt. Pinatubo aerosol spikes from skewing the result.

4. Other features

Judge sandbox (JUDGE / SETTINGS): all five floors of the elevator are unlocked from the start. The settings menu also has an “Unlock All 5 Evidence Cards & Open Evidence Wall” button for testing the end-game synthesis right away.

Dr. Nova and ORBIT AI have a custom six-expression sprite system (Neutral, Explaining, Thinking, Concerned, Surprised, Happy). Commander Atlas and Junior Detective Steve have custom portraits.

All audio is synthesized live through the browser’s AudioContext, so the game needs no audio files. This covers the ambient space chords, typewriter blips, radar sweeps, and airlock doors.

Players can edit their synthesis notes and copy a formatted text dossier of their findings to the clipboard.

Global Ozone Trend Detection Map (2005–2024)

A global spatial distribution map illustrating long-term ozone trends across different latitudes and longitudes from 2005 to 2024. Blue regions indicate decreasing trends, while red regions represent increasing trends. Black dots highlight grid cells with statistically significant trends after False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. The map reveals distinct regional variations in ozone trends across the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

Long-Term Atmospheric Trends (2005–2024)

A multi-line time-series visualization showing standardized environmental anomalies across five atmospheric layers: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, and Exosphere. Each colored line represents annual variations, while the dashed lines indicate the corresponding long-term linear trends. The visualization highlights contrasting atmospheric behaviors, with some layers exhibiting increasing anomalies and others showing decreasing trends over the study period.

Mann–Kendall-Style Statistical Trend Analysis

A statistical summary of the long-term trend analysis using Theil–Sen slope estimation and Kendall's tau. The results indicate a statistically significant decreasing trend, with a Theil–Sen slope of −0.06731, a 95% confidence interval of −0.09318 to −0.04646, Kendall's tau of −0.6737, and a p-value of 0.000000. These findings provide statistical evidence supporting the observed decreasing trend.

Comparative Atmospheric Trend Estimation

Comparative estimation of long-term environmental trends across five atmospheric layers using Theil–Sen robust slope estimation. Horizontal error bars represent 95% confidence intervals, and statistical significance is assessed using Kendall trend testing with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction.
